claim: Free-living and obligate intracellular bacteria are both polarized.
source: Although free-living and obligate intracellular bacteria are both polarized it is unclear whether the underlying polarization mechanisms and effector proteins are conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information for the study.

claim: The NMR solution structure of the zinc-finger (ZnR) domain from ZitP revealed conserved interaction determinants for PopZ.
source: The NMR solution structure of the zinc-finger (ZnR) domain from the bifunctional and bipolar ZitP pilus assembly/motility regulator revealed conserved interaction determinants for PopZ, a bipolar matrix protein that anchors the ParB centromere-binding protein and other regulatory factors at the poles.
evidence: The abstract states that the NMR structure was determined and revealed interaction determinants.

claim: PopZ is a bipolar matrix protein that anchors the ParB centromere-binding protein and other regulatory factors at the poles.
source: The NMR solution structure of the zinc-finger (ZnR) domain from the bifunctional and bipolar ZitP pilus assembly/motility regulator revealed conserved interaction determinants for PopZ, a bipolar matrix protein that anchors the ParB centromere-binding protein and other regulatory factors at the poles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PopZ function.

claim: ZitP regulates cytokinesis.
source: We show that ZitP regulates cytokinesis and the localization of ParB and PopZ, targeting PopZ independently of the previously known binding sites for its client proteins.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding of the study.

claim: ZitP regulates the localization of ParB and PopZ.
source: We show that ZitP regulates cytokinesis and the localization of ParB and PopZ, targeting PopZ independently of the previously known binding sites for its client proteins.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding of the study.

claim: ZitP targets PopZ independently of the previously known binding sites for its client proteins.
source: We show that ZitP regulates cytokinesis and the localization of ParB and PopZ, targeting PopZ independently of the previously known binding sites for its client proteins.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding of the study.

claim: The (bi-)polarization system is conserved in free-living and obligate intracellular α-proteobacteria.
source: Through heterologous localization assays with rickettsial ZitP and PopZ orthologs, we document the shared ancestries, activities and structural determinants of a (bi-)polarization system encoded in free-living and obligate intracellular α-proteobacteria.
evidence: The abstract states this as a conclusion from heterologous localization assays.

claim: Distinct polarization mechanisms exist in different bacterial phyla.
source: Cell pole-organizing proteins arose more than once during bacterial evolution as indicated by the fact that distinct polarization mechanisms exist in different bacterial phyla (Davis and Waldor, 2013; Kirkpatrick and Viollier, 2011; Strahl and Hamoen, 2012; Treuner-Lange and Søgaard-Andersen, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Gram-negative α-proteobacterial lineage encompasses polarized free-living and obligate intracellular bacteria including the mitochondrial ancestors.
source: The Gram-negative α-proteobacterial lineage encompasses polarized free-living (Davis and Waldor, 2013; Haglund et al., 2010; Hallez et al., 2004; Kirkpatrick and Viollier, 2011) and obligate intracellular bacteria including the mitochondrial ancestors (Andersson et al., 1998; Haglund et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus is a model system for the genetic analysis of α-proteobacterial cell polarity.
source: The fresh-water bacterium Caulobacter crescentus is a model system for the genetic analysis of α-proteobacterial cell polarity because polar differentiation is tightly coordinated with cell cycle progression and because of the availability of a myriad of genetic tools to study this species compared to the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) pathogens (Figure 1A)(Curtis and Brun, 2010; Ely, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C. crescentus predivisional cell features the flagellum and a pilus biosynthesis machine at the new pole and a stalk at the old pole.
source: The C. crescentus predivisional cell features the flagellum and a pilus biosynthesis machine at the new pole and a stalk, a cylindrical extension of the cell envelope, at the old pole.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell structure.

claim: The replicative stalked (ST) cell progeny begins chromosome replication and an asymmetric cell division cycle upon completion of cell division.
source: Upon completion of cell division, the replicative stalked (ST) cell progeny begins chromosome replication and an asymmetric cell division cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell cycle.

claim: The motile and piliated swarmer (SW) cell progeny resides temporarily in a non-replicative (G1-like) state.
source: By contrast, the motile and piliated swarmer (SW) cell progeny resides temporarily in a non-replicative (G1-like) state.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell cycle.

claim: At the SW to ST cell transition, the flagellated and piliated (SW) pole is remodeled into a ST pole and the developing cell acquires DNA replication competence.
source: At the SW to ST cell transition, the flagellated and piliated (SW) pole is remodeled into a ST pole and the developing cell acquires DNA replication competence.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. crescentus cell cycle.

claim: Replication of the circular chromosome proceeds bi-directionally from the single origin of replication (Cori) located at the nascent ST pole.
source: Replication of the circular chromosome proceeds bi-directionally from the single origin of replication (Cori) located at the nascent ST pole (Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Once duplicated, the Cori region is rapidly segregated towards the nascent SW pole by the ParAB chromosome segregation system.
source: Once duplicated, the Cori region is rapidly segregated towards the nascent SW pole by the ParAB chromosome segregation system that targets the parS centromeric sequence located circa 8 kbp from Cori (Figure 1A)(Mohl and Gober, 1997; Viollier et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The parS centromeric sequence is located circa 8 kbp from Cori.
source: Once duplicated, the Cori region is rapidly segregated towards the nascent SW pole by the ParAB chromosome segregation system that targets the parS centromeric sequence located circa 8 kbp from Cori (Figure 1A)(Mohl and Gober, 1997; Viollier et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The cis-encoded ParB protein binds parS.
source: The cis-encoded ParB protein binds parS and the resulting ParB•parS complex is guided pole-ward by the ParA ATPase, likely reinforced by poorly understood biophysical constraints and properties of the chromosome (Lim et al., 2014; Mohl and Gober, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ParB•parS complex is guided pole-ward by the ParA ATPase.
source: The cis-encoded ParB protein binds parS and the resulting ParB•parS complex is guided pole-ward by the ParA ATPase, likely reinforced by poorly understood biophysical constraints and properties of the chromosome (Lim et al., 2014; Mohl and Gober, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PopZ is thought to assemble a porous homo-polymeric matrix at the cell poles that captures the segregated ParB•parS complex.
source: The PopZ polar organizing protein is thought to assemble a porous homo-polymeric matrix at the cell poles that captures the segregated ParB•parS complex (Figure 1A) via a direct interaction with ParAB (Bowman et al., 2008, 2013; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PopZ captures the segregated ParB•parS complex via a direct interaction with ParAB.
source: The PopZ polar organizing protein is thought to assemble a porous homo-polymeric matrix at the cell poles that captures the segregated ParB•parS complex (Figure 1A) via a direct interaction with ParAB (Bowman et al., 2008, 2013; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In newborn cells PopZ is localized to the old cell pole, whereas the newborn pole initially lacks a PopZ cluster.
source: The polar localization of PopZ is cell cycle-regulated: in newborn cells PopZ is localized to the old cell pole, whereas the newborn pole initially lacks a PopZ cluster (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During S-phase, PopZ adopts a bipolar disposition coincident with ParB•parS segregation.
source: During S-phase, PopZ adopts a bipolar disposition (Figure 1A) coincident with ParB•parS segregation to facilitate its capture at the opposite pole.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Formation of the second polar PopZ cluster may depend on the ParA ATPase and the TipN landmark protein.
source: Formation of the second polar PopZ cluster may depend on the ParA ATPase and the TipN landmark protein, a coiled-coil protein that interacts with ParA and that marks the new pole as flagellar assembly site (Huitema et al., 2006; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Lam et al., 2006; Ptacin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: TipN is a coiled-coil protein that interacts with ParA and marks the new pole as flagellar assembly site.
source: Formation of the second polar PopZ cluster may depend on the ParA ATPase and the TipN landmark protein, a coiled-coil protein that interacts with ParA and that marks the new pole as flagellar assembly site (Huitema et al., 2006; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Lam et al., 2006; Ptacin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus.
source: Although ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus, TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Mohl and Gober, 1997), but joint inactivation of both genes arrests growth (Schofield et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable in C. crescentus.
source: Although ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus, TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Mohl and Gober, 1997), but joint inactivation of both genes arrests growth (Schofield et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Joint inactivation of TipN and PopZ arrests growth in C. crescentus.
source: Although ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus, TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Mohl and Gober, 1997), but joint inactivation of both genes arrests growth (Schofield et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB, but not TipN.
source: As most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB, but not TipN, TipN-independent control mechanism(s) for PopZ polarization should exist in α-proteobacteria.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that leads to an inference.

claim: TipN-independent control mechanism(s) for PopZ polarization should exist in α-proteobacteria.
source: As most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB, but not TipN, TipN-independent control mechanism(s) for PopZ polarization should exist in α-proteobacteria.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on genomic observations.

claim: In the Rhizobiales order, PopZ does not appear to fasten ParB at the cell poles as polar PopZ does not co-localize with ParB.
source: In the Rhizobiales order of the α-proteobacteria, PopZ does not appear to fasten ParB at the cell poles as polar PopZ does not co-localize with ParB: while PopZ is monopolar, ParB localizes in a bipolar fashion (Deghelt et al., 2014; Grangeon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Rhizobiales, PopZ is monopolar while ParB localizes in a bipolar fashion.
source: In the Rhizobiales order of the α-proteobacteria, PopZ does not appear to fasten ParB at the cell poles as polar PopZ does not co-localize with ParB: while PopZ is monopolar, ParB localizes in a bipolar fashion (Deghelt et al., 2014; Grangeon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PopZ has undergone functional specialization in the Rhizobiales, presumably interacting with other (unknown) client proteins.
source: Thus, compared to the bipolar co-localization of PopZ and ParB observed in C. crescentus (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Ptacin et al., 2014), PopZ seems to have undergone functional specialization in the Rhizobiales, presumably interacting with other (unknown) client proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on localization differences.

claim: The genomes of the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) lineage encode PopZ and ParAB orthologs.
source: The genomes of the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) lineage also encode PopZ and ParAB orthologs (Andersson et al., 1998), but not several other known client proteins of C. crescentus PopZ that depend on a short N-terminal stretch in PopZ to interact with it (Bowman et al., 2010; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rickettsial genomes do not encode several other known client proteins of C. crescentus PopZ that depend on a short N-terminal stretch in PopZ to interact with it.
source: The genomes of the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) lineage also encode PopZ and ParAB orthologs (Andersson et al., 1998), but not several other known client proteins of C. crescentus PopZ that depend on a short N-terminal stretch in PopZ to interact with it (Bowman et al., 2010; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There is a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP.
source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: ZitP is a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein.
source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C-terminal DUF3426 domain of ZitP is required for polar pilus biogenesis.
source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C-terminal DUF3426 domain of ZitP is dispensable for motility.
source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The PopZ•ZitP interaction is required to control cytokinesis and centromere positioning from the membrane.
source: We locate the structural determinants governing PopZ•ZitP complex formation and we show that this interaction is required to control cytokinesis and centromere positioning from the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The PopZ•ZitP interaction does not require the PopZ N-terminal segment that is used by other client proteins.
source: The PopZ•ZitP interaction differs for previously described interactions between PopZ and client proteins (Holmes et al., 2016) in that it does not require the aforementioned PopZ N-terminal segment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host Escherichia coli.
source: We show that ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host Escherichia coli and we reconstitute a bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex in this system.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: A bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex can be reconstituted in E. coli.
source: We show that ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host Escherichia coli and we reconstitute a bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex in this system.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The PopZ•ZitP complex is modular.
source: Examining rickettsial PopZ and ZitP orthologs, we find that the PopZ•ZitP complex is modular and that the structure-function relationship is maintained in the obligate intracellular lineage.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The structure-function relationship of the PopZ•ZitP complex is maintained in the obligate intracellular lineage.
source: Examining rickettsial PopZ and ZitP orthologs, we find that the PopZ•ZitP complex is modular and that the structure-function relationship is maintained in the obligate intracellular lineage.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: A C. crescentus strain bearing a Tn5-GFP insertion in the 5'-proximal third of the CC_2215/CCNA_02298 gene (zitP) expresses a bipolarly localized and truncated ZitP-GFP fusion protein and is viable.
source: We previously isolated a C. crescentus strain bearing a Tn5-GFP insertion in the 5'-proximal third of the poorly characterized and conserved CC_2215/CCNA_02298 gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, dubbed zitP, zinc-finger targeting PopZ, Figure 1B–D). The resulting strain expresses a bipolarly localized and truncated ZitP-GFP fusion protein and is viable (Hughes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding supported by citation.

claim: Genome-wide transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-Seq) revealed that ZitP is not essential for viability, but required for pilus biogenesis and motility.
source: Consistent with this result, genome-wide transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-Seq) revealed that ZitP is not essential for viability, but required for pilus biogenesis and motility (Christen et al., 2011, 2016; Hughes et al., 2010)(Mignolet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37).
source: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37, henceforth ZnR, Figure 1B–C) and a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127) preceding the C-terminal DUF3426 (residues 128–245).
evidence: This is stated as a structural prediction.

claim: ZitP has a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127).
source: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37, henceforth ZnR, Figure 1B–C) and a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127) preceding the C-terminal DUF3426 (residues 128–245).
evidence: This is stated as a structural prediction.

claim: ZitP has a C-terminal DUF3426 domain (residues 128–245).
source: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37, henceforth ZnR, Figure 1B–C) and a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127) preceding the C-terminal DUF3426 (residues 128–245).
evidence: This is stated as a structural prediction.

claim: The DUF3426 is required for polar pilus biogenesis but not required for motility or to direct ZitP to the cell poles.
source: While the DUF3426 is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016), it is not required for motility or to direct ZitP to the cell poles since in polar ZitPTn-GFP the GFP moiety is fused in-frame to codon 49 of ZitP (green triangle in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding combining previous knowledge and current observation.

claim: Quantitative live-cell fluorescence imaging of ZitPTn-GFP in zitP::Tn5-GFP cells (n = 1048) revealed monopolar fluorescent foci in non-constricted cells, while bipolar foci are present in constricted cells.
source: Quantitative live-cell fluorescence imaging of ZitPTn-GFP in zitP::Tn5-GFP cells (n = 1048) revealed monopolar fluorescent foci in non-constricted cells, while bipolar foci are present in constricted cells (Figure 1D), suggesting that the ZnR and/or adjacent residues are necessary and sufficient for ZitP polarization and that bipolarization is cell cycle-regulated.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ZnR and/or adjacent residues are necessary and sufficient for ZitP polarization and bipolarization is cell cycle-regulated.
source: Quantitative live-cell fluorescence imaging of ZitPTn-GFP in zitP::Tn5-GFP cells (n = 1048) revealed monopolar fluorescent foci in non-constricted cells, while bipolar foci are present in constricted cells (Figure 1D), suggesting that the ZnR and/or adjacent residues are necessary and sufficient for ZitP polarization and that bipolarization is cell cycle-regulated.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the imaging data.

claim: Residues 1–90 of ZitP carry the necessary information for polar localization of ZitP.
source: We engineered strains expressing a Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) fusion protein (an N-terminal translational fusion of the Dendra2 fluorescent protein to only the cytoplasmic part of ZitP) from the xylose-inducible promoter (Pxyl) at the xylX locus in the wild-type (WT, NA1000) or ΔzitP background and found an identical localization pattern as for the ZitPTn-GFP strain, indicating that residues 1–90 carry the necessary information for polar localization of ZitP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Orthologous Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) variants from other α-proteobacteria show an identical localization pattern when expressed in C. crescentus.
source: To test if polarization is also a feature of ZitP from other α-proteobacteria, we expressed orthologous Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) variants in WT or ΔzitP C. crescentus cells and observed an identical localization pattern of these fusion proteins (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The zinc-finger domain from the unrelated AgmX protein encoded in the δ-proteobacterium Myxococcus xanthus is not polar in C. crescentus.
source: By contrast, the zinc-finger domain from the unrelated AgmX protein encoded in the δ-proteobacterium Myxococcus xanthus (Nan et al., 2010) is not polar in C. crescentus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the zinc-finger domain of AgmX diverged.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 43 residues encompassing the C. crescentus ZitP ZnR domain suffice to direct Dendra2 to the cell poles.
source: Next, we asked if the highly conserved 43 residues encompassing the C. crescentus ZitP ZnR domain (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) suffice to direct Dendra2 to the cell poles. Expression of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) from xylX in C. crescentus WT or ΔzitP cells indeed gave rise to cell cycle-dependent bipolar fluorescence (Figure 1G)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is initially monopolar in G1-phase cells and switches to a bipolar disposition during S-phase, 60 min after the release of G1 cells into fresh medium.
source: This ZnR interacts directly with PopZ and controls its localization from the membrane, even when PopZ no longer carries the interaction sites for ParAB, indicating that PopZ localization is regulated by redundant mechanisms in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1G.

claim: mCherry-PopZ co-localizes with Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in ΔzitP cells.
source: Since this cell cycle localization pattern of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) closely resembles that of the polar matrix protein PopZ (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008), we co-expressed Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and mCherry-PopZ in ΔzitP (xylX::dendra-zitP1-43popZ::mCherry-popZ) cells and found that mCherry-PopZ co-localizes with Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from co-localization experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: ZitPTn-GFP, Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) and Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) are all delocalized (diffuse) in ΔpopZ cells.
source: Importantly, ZitPTn-GFP, Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) and Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) are all delocalized (diffuse) in ΔpopZ cells (Figure 1D, E and F) and immunoblotting revealed that the abundance of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is not significantly affected by the ΔpopZ mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figures 1D, E, F and immunoblotting in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The abundance of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is not significantly affected by the ΔpopZ mutation.
source: Importantly, ZitPTn-GFP, Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) and Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) are all delocalized (diffuse) in ΔpopZ cells (Figure 1D, E and F) and immunoblotting revealed that the abundance of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is not significantly affected by the ΔpopZ mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and full length Dendra2-ZitP adopt a monopolar 'plug'-like disposition when PopZ is overexpressed.
source: We observed Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and full length Dendra2-ZitP to adopt a monopolar 'plug'-like disposition when PopZ is overexpressed (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is indeed recruited to PopZ 'plugs'.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ZitP(1-43) and PopZ can be co-purified by SEC and the resulting ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex has a high apparent molecular mass.
source: ZitP(1-43) and PopZ can be co-purified by SEC and the resulting ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex has a high apparent molecular mass, suggesting that ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from SEC experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ.
source: ZitP(1-43) and PopZ can be co-purified by SEC and the resulting ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex has a high apparent molecular mass, suggesting that ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from SEC data.

claim: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) estimated the dissociation constant (KD) between ZitP(1-43) and PopZ at 700 nM.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) estimated the dissociation constant (KD) between ZitP(1-43) and PopZ at 700 nM (Figure 2C), confirming the specific interaction between both proteins in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The 20 NMR structures of ZitP(1-43) were overlaid with a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over the backbone atoms.
source: The 20 NMR structures of ZitP(1-43) were overlaid with a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over the backbone atoms (Supplementary file 1), revealing two double-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (ββαββ), forming a 'crab claw' in which C5, C8, C28, C31 are located at the turns of β1/β2 and β3/β4 chelate a zinc ion (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from NMR structure determination shown in Figure 2D-E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The ZitP ZnR structure reveals two double-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (ββαββ), forming a 'crab claw' in which C5, C8, C28, C31 chelate a zinc ion.
source: The 20 NMR structures of ZitP(1-43) were overlaid with a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over the backbone atoms (Supplementary file 1), revealing two double-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (ββαββ), forming a 'crab claw' in which C5, C8, C28, C31 are located at the turns of β1/β2 and β3/β4 chelate a zinc ion (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from NMR structure determination shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The ZitP ZnR structure is unusual, though related to the family of the 'ribbon zinc-fingers' (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily), albeit it lacks the additional β-strand typically located in between the two β-sheets.
source: This ZitP ZnR structure is unusual, though related to the family of the 'ribbon zinc-fingers' (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily), albeit it lacks the additional β-strand typically located in between the two β-sheets.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: W35 in ZitP is required to bind PopZ in vitro, as determined by ITC with a W35I mutant derivative of ZitP(1-43).
source: Moreover, W35 is surrounded by a surface-exposed patch of basic residues (K18, R24, R27, R34, Figure 2E) and it is required to bind PopZ in vitro, as determined by ITC with a W35I mutant derivative of ZitP(1-43) [ZitP(1-43)W35I, Figure 2C].
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: W35I impairs the interaction of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) with polar PopZ in vivo.
source: Consistent with these ITC experiments, W35I impairs the interaction of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) with polar PopZ in vivo (Figure 3A and B), as indicated by the diffuse fluorescence of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus and in E. coli cells expressing PopZ (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: A C5S/C8S/C28S/C31S quadruple or a R24A/R27A double mutation both disrupt polarization of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells.
source: Similarly, a C5S/C8S/C28S/C31S quadruple or a R24A/R27A double mutation both disrupt polarization of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: All of the substituted Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) variants are stably expressed.
source: As all of the substituted Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) variants are stably expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we conclude that these residues are required for the formation of a polar ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunoblotting shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: W35, the basic patch and the integrity of the Zn2+ coordinating center are required for the formation of a polar ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex.
source: As all of the substituted Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) variants are stably expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we conclude that these residues are required for the formation of a polar ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutagenesis and localization data.

claim: R. sphaeroides Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is largely diffuse in C. crescentus or in PopZ-expressing E. coli, but some faint polar signals are noticeable.
source: Interestingly, R. sphaeroides Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is also largely diffuse in C. crescentus (Figure 3C) or in PopZ-expressing E. coli, but some faint polar signals are noticeable as well (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The 'corrected' R. sphaeroides ZitP(1-43)Q27R version is robustly polar in C. crescentus and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells.
source: We therefore asked if polar localization could be improved if this substitution is 'corrected' (i.e. reversed) by a Q27R substitution of R. sphaeroides Dendra2-ZitP(1-43). This 'corrected' R. sphaeroides ZitP(1-43)Q27R version is indeed robustly polar in C. crescentus (Figure 3C) and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: When the W35I substitution is introduced into the 'corrected' R. sphaeroides variant, polar localization is again lost without compromising abundance.
source: When the W35I substitution is introduced into this 'corrected' R. sphaeroides variant, polar localization is again lost without compromising abundance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ChIP-Seq experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo.
source: To this end, we conducted chromatin immunoprecipitation-deep-sequencing (ChIP-Seq) using antibodies recognizing ParB (anti-ParB) or ZitP (anti-ZitP specific for either the N-terminus or the C-terminus, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). These experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking, but not overlapping, parS (by 2–3 kpb).
source: These experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo and additionally showed that i) the ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking, but not overlapping, parS (by 2–3 kpb) and that ii) the ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for this association (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for the association of the ZitP•PopZ complex with chromosomal regions flanking parS.
source: These experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo and additionally showed that i) the ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking, but not overlapping, parS (by 2–3 kpb) and that ii) the ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for this association (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inactivation of ZitP has a mild effect on CFP-ParB localization in WT cells.
source: While inactivation of ZitP has a mild effect on CFP-ParB localization in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we observed aberrant CFP-ParB localization and perturbed cytokinesis in ΔzitP cells expressing variants of PopZ impaired in binding ParB and/or ParA (Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014)(Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aberrant CFP-ParB localization and perturbed cytokinesis are observed in ΔzitP cells expressing variants of PopZ impaired in binding ParB and/or ParA.
source: While inactivation of ZitP has a mild effect on CFP-ParB localization in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we observed aberrant CFP-ParB localization and perturbed cytokinesis in ΔzitP cells expressing variants of PopZ impaired in binding ParB and/or ParA (Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014)(Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing mCherry-PopZKE had fewer bipolar foci compared to zitP+ cells and an increase of cells without polar signals.
source: Quantification revealed that ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing mCherry-PopZKE (impaired in ParB binding, ΔzitP mCherry-popZKE) had fewer bipolar foci compared to zitP+ cells and an increase of cells without polar signals.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantification of localization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ZitP promotes polar localization of PopZ when the ParAB-dependent localization pathway is impaired.
source: Importantly, these abnormalities were not seen in zitP+ cells, indicating that ZitP promotes polar localization of PopZ when the ParAB-dependent (and/or another) localization pathway requiring the PopZ N-terminal region is impaired.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the localization data.

claim: The efficiency of plating (EOP) of ΔzitP cells harboring the popZΔ26 allele is markedly reduced compared to zitP+ cells.
source: Consistent with these results, we found that the efficiency of plating (EOP) of ΔzitP cells harboring the popZΔ26 allele (ΔzitP mCherry-popZΔ26) that encodes a PopZ variant lacking the N-terminal 26 residues to bind ParAB and other client proteins (Holmes et al., 2016; Ptacin et al., 2014) is markedly reduced compared to zitP+ cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from EOP assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: EOP was similarly diminished in ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing PopZKEP.
source: EOP was similarly diminished in ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing PopZKEP (ΔzitP mCherry-popZKEP) a version of PopZ in which the interaction sites for ParAB (and other PopZ client proteins) are inactivated by site-directed muatgenesis [E12K/R19E/S22P](Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from EOP assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The C-terminal DUF3426 that is required for polar pilus biogenesis is not required to improve growth in ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing mCherry-PopZKE.
source: While exploring which region in ZitP is required to control PopZ, we noted that ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing the mCherry-PopZKE have a reduced growth rate in broth and that this defect is rescued by expression of (full-length) Dendra2-ZitP from the xylX locus using the xylose-inducible Pxyl promoter (Figure 4C). The C-terminal DUF3426 that is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016) is not required to improve growth , as revealed by growth measurements of cells expressing the ZitP(1-133) variant.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from growth measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the interaction with PopZ is abrogated in the ZitP(1-133W35I) mutant, cells grow poorly.
source: However, when the interaction with PopZ is abrogated [in the ZitP(1-133W35I) mutant], cells grow poorly.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from growth measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No dependency on ZitP is seen in ΔpopZ cells expressing otherwise unmodified mCherry-PopZ.
source: By contrast, no dependency on ZitP is seen in ΔpopZ cells expressing otherwise unmodified mCherry-PopZ (mCherry-popZ, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from growth measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ZitP is important for growth and viability for ΔpopZ cells expressing PopZ that no longer interacts efficiently with ParAB.
source: Taken together, these results show that ZitP is important for growth and viability for ΔpopZ cells expressing PopZ that no longer interacts efficiently with ParAB, and that the ability of membrane-anchored ZitP to bind PopZ via the ZnR is important to regulate PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the growth and localization data.

claim: The ability of membrane-anchored ZitP to bind PopZ via the ZnR is important to regulate PopZ.
source: Taken together, these results show that ZitP is important for growth and viability for ΔpopZ cells expressing PopZ that no longer interacts efficiently with ParAB, and that the ability of membrane-anchored ZitP to bind PopZ via the ZnR is important to regulate PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the growth and localization data.

claim: There exist at least two (redundant) mechanisms of PopZ localization control in C. crescentus: one regulated directly or indirectly by ParAB and another that is modulated by membrane-anchored ZitP.
source: Thus, there exist at least two (redundant) mechanisms of PopZ localization control in C. crescentus: one regulated directly or indirectly by ParAB (Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014) (or the N-terminal region of PopZ) and another that is modulated by membrane-anchored ZitP [ZitP(1-133)].
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic and localization data.

claim: Localization of ParB and PopZ is strongly perturbed upon induction of ZitP(1-133) with xylose in cfp-parB mCherry-popZ cells.
source: Further insight for the role of this truncated (membrane-anchored) ZitP came from overexpression of ZitP(1-133) from Pxyl on a multi-copy plasmid (pMT464) in cfp-parB mCherry-popZ cells. We found that localization of ParB and PopZ is strongly perturbed (Figure 4D) upon induction of ZitP(1-133) with xylose.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Time lapse-fluorescence imaging revealed that the pole-ward movement of CFP-ParB normally seen in S-phase of WT cells stalls halfway through in cells overexpressing ZitP(1-133).
source: Time lapse-fluorescence imaging revealed that the pole-ward movement of CFP-ParB normally seen in S-phase of WT cells stalls halfway through in cells overexpressing ZitP(1-133) (Figure 4D, see Figure 4—figure supplement 3A for GFP-ParB).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In cells overexpressing ZitP(1-133), mCherry-PopZ forms internal clusters, often proximal to CFP-ParB clusters.
source: In these cells, mCherry-PopZ forms internal clusters, often proximal to CFP-ParB clusters.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CFP-ParB movement and mCherry-PopZ localization proceeds normally through the cell cycle in cells overexpressing the W35I derivative of ZitP(1-133).
source: By contrast, CFP-ParB movement and mCherry-PopZ localization proceeds normally through the cell cycle in cells overexpressing the W35I derivative of ZitP(1-133) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ZitP(1-133) overexpression displaces a monomeric ParA derivative [ParA(G16V)] from the cell poles into aberrant cytoplasmic clusters.
source: Also, ZitP(1-133) overexpression displaces a monomeric ParA derivative [ParA(G16V)] whose localization is PopZ-dependent (Ptacin et al., 2014) from the cell poles into aberrant cytoplasmic clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Overexpression of ZitP(1-133) causes cell filamentation at the population level.
source: These defects seen at the single cell level are accompanied by cell filamentation at the population level and are not apparent either with full-length ZitP (Figure 4E) overexpressed to comparable levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C) or with ZitP(1-133) variants harboring the W35I single mutation, the R24A/R27A double mutation or the C5S/C8S/C28S/C31S quadruple mutation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from microscopy observations shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpression of the ZnR without any membrane anchoring domain [ZitP(1-90)] does not cause cell cycle defects.
source: As overexpression of the ZnR without any membrane anchoring domain [ZitP(1-90)] does not cause such cell cycle defects either (Figure 4F), we asked if membrane-anchoring is specific for this ZitP activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The overexpression phenotypes are still supported by overexpression of a ZitP version in which the TM of ZitP(1-133) had been replaced with an unrelated TM from the E. coli MalF protein.
source: The aforementioned overexpression phenotypes are still supported by overexpression of a ZitP version in which the TM of ZitP(1-133) had been replaced with an unrelated TM from the E. coli MalF protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Overproduction of ZitP1-133 in mCherry-popZKEP cells recapitulates the overexpression phenotype seen in mCherry-popZ cells.
source: Finally, we also observed that overproduction of ZitP1-133 in mCherry-popZKEP cells [in which the interaction with ParAB is impaired, (Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014) recapitulates the overxpression phenotype (Figure 4G) seen in mCherry-popZ cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Membrane-anchored ZitP robustly and directly controls PopZ localization in E. coli and in C. crescentus.
source: As biochemical fractionation experiments confirmed the predicted localization of ZitP(1-43) and ZitP(1-133) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), we conclude that membrane-anchored ZitP robustly and directly controls PopZ localization in E. coli and in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the localization and fractionation data.

claim: ZitP(1-120) from Brevundimonas diminuta and ZitP(1-104) from Rickettsia massiliae induced filamentation with mislocalized CFP-ParB and mCherry-PopZ when overexpressed in C. crescentus.
source: To investigate if the ZitP-dependent control of PopZ localization is common to closely and distantly related α-proteobacterial lineages, we overexpressed ZitP(1-120) from Brevundimonas diminuta and ZitP(1-104) from Rickettsia massiliae [corresponding to C. crescentus ZitP(1-133)] in C. crescentus and found that both induced filamentation with mislocalized CFP-ParB and mCherry-PopZ akin to C. crescentus ZitP(1-133) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ZitP(1-104)Rm prevents the accumulation of monopolar 'plugs' of overexpressed PopZCc in C. crescentus.
source: As for C. crescentus ZitP or ZitP(1-133) (Figure 5E), ZitP(1-104)Rm prevents the accumulation of monopolar 'plugs' of overexpressed PopZCc in C. crescentus (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: R. massiliae ZnR [ZitP(1-43)Rm] localizes to the C. crescentus cell poles in a PopZ-dependent manner, but no longer when the analogous W35I mutation is introduced.
source: As expected, this R. massiliae ZnR [ZitP(1-43)Rm] also localizes to the C. crescentus cell poles in a PopZ-dependent manner, but no longer when the analogous W35I mutation is introduced (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Rickettsial ZnR co-localizes with C. crescentus mCherry-PopZ in E. coli.
source: Rickettsial ZnR also co-localizes with C. crescentus mCherry-PopZ in E. coli (Figure 6D) and ZitP(1-104)Rm directs mCherry-PopZ into bipolarity (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ZitP(1-104)Rm directs mCherry-PopZ into bipolarity in E. coli.
source: Rickettsial ZnR also co-localizes with C. crescentus mCherry-PopZ in E. coli (Figure 6D) and ZitP(1-104)Rm directs mCherry-PopZ into bipolarity (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: R. massiliae PopZ can recruit C. crescentus Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) to clusters in E. coli.
source: Finally, we found that i) R. massiliae PopZ can also recruit C. crescentus Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) to clusters in E. coli (Figure 6F) and that ii) it promotes the bipolar localization of full-length Dendra2-ZitP (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: R. massiliae PopZ promotes the bipolar localization of full-length C. crescentus Dendra2-ZitP in E. coli.
source: Finally, we found that i) R. massiliae PopZ can also recruit C. crescentus Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) to clusters in E. coli (Figure 6F) and that ii) it promotes the bipolar localization of full-length Dendra2-ZitP (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The PopZ-ZitP bipartite bipolarization system is conserved in α-proteobacteria and modular.
source: We conclude that the PopZ-ZitP bipartite bipolarization system is conserved in α-proteobacteria and modular.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the heterologous localization experiments.

claim: Eukaryotic zinc-finger (ZnR) domains are typically used to bind DNA, but they can also mediate protein-protein interactions.
source: Eukaryotic zinc-finger (ZnR) domains are typically used to bind DNA, but they can also mediate protein-protein interactions (Klug, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The ZitP ZnR acts as a conserved polar localization sequence by promoting the interaction with the PopZ polar organizer of α-proteobacteria.
source: Here we described a small (43-residue) ZnR that acts as a conserved polar localization sequence, reminiscent of the nuclear localization signal (NLS) of eukaryotes, by promoting the interaction with the PopZ polar organizer of α-proteobacteria.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The ZitP ZnR interacts directly with PopZ and controls its localization from the membrane, even when PopZ no longer carries the interaction sites for ParAB.
source: This ZnR interacts directly with PopZ and controls its localization from the membrane, even when PopZ no longer carries the interaction sites for ParAB, indicating that PopZ localization is regulated by redundant mechanisms in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: PopZ localization is regulated by redundant mechanisms in C. crescentus.
source: This ZnR interacts directly with PopZ and controls its localization from the membrane, even when PopZ no longer carries the interaction sites for ParAB, indicating that PopZ localization is regulated by redundant mechanisms in C. crescentus.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: One mechanism of PopZ localization may require ParAB or at least it depends on the N-terminal region of PopZ that promotes the interaction with ParAB and other PopZ client proteins.
source: One mechanism may require ParAB or at least it depends on the N-terminal region of PopZ that promotes the interaction with ParAB and other PopZ client proteins (Holmes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: ZitP controls PopZ independently of the N-terminal region of PopZ, underscoring the multivalent interactions and multifunctional properties of PopZ.
source: However, ZitP controls PopZ independently of this region, underscoring the multivalent interactions and multifunctional properties of PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: ZitP emerges as a new component of the α-proteobacterial polarity control pathway using an N-terminal ZnR to regulate PopZ localization.
source: ZitP emerges as new a component of the α-proteobacterial polarity control pathway using an N-terminal ZnR to regulate PopZ localization.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: ZitP is bifunctional, controlling the localization of polar pilus biogenesis proteins via its C-terminal DUF3426.
source: Interestingly, ZitP is bifunctional, controlling the localization of polar pilus biogenesis proteins via its C-terminal DUF3426 (Mignolet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The DUF3426 is less conserved among the α-proteobacteria and dispensable for PopZ localization control.
source: While the DUF3426 is less conserved among the α-proteobacteria and dispensable for PopZ localization control, the membrane-anchored ZitP ZnR and PopZ binding is featured by many ZitP orthologs from the branch of obligate intracellular α-proteobacteria (the Rickettsiae) and regulates PopZ subcellular positioning.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The membrane-anchored ZitP ZnR and PopZ binding is featured by many ZitP orthologs from the branch of obligate intracellular α-proteobacteria (the Rickettsiae) and regulates PopZ subcellular positioning.
source: While the DUF3426 is less conserved among the α-proteobacteria and dispensable for PopZ localization control, the membrane-anchored ZitP ZnR and PopZ binding is featured by many ZitP orthologs from the branch of obligate intracellular α-proteobacteria (the Rickettsiae) and regulates PopZ subcellular positioning.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: PopZ-bound ZitP associates indirectly with sites flanking the ParB-bound centromere (parS), rather than parS itself.
source: An unexpected finding was that PopZ-bound ZitP associates indirectly with sites flanking the ParB-bound centromere (parS), rather than parS itself that ParB binds (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction between PopZ and ParAB, or at least the N-terminal region of PopZ, is required for ZitP to associate with parS-flanking sites.
source: We found that the interaction between PopZ and ParAB (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014, 2010), or at least the N-terminal region of PopZ, is required for ZitP to associate with these parS-flanking sites.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments.

claim: ZitP is well positioned to exert control of ParB•parS dynamics and to impair segregation by sequestering the adjacent centromere into aberrant PopZ•ZitP clusters.
source: With the juxtaposition of PopZ•ZitP at the ParB-bound centromere and our reconstitution of the ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex in E. coli, ZitP is well positioned to exert control of ParB•parS dynamics and to impair segregation by sequestering the adjacent centromere into aberrant PopZ•ZitP clusters.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The ParB-control function of PopZ•ZitP depends on the ability of membrane-anchored ZitP ZnR to interact with PopZ.
source: The ParB-control function of PopZ•ZitP depends on the ability of membrane-anchored ZitP ZnR to interact with PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: ZitP targets residues flanking the conserved C-terminal DUF2497 of PopZ.
source: Our molecular dissections provide evidence that ZitP targets residues flanking the conserved C-terminal DUF2497 of PopZ.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the molecular dissection experiments.

claim: The DUF2497 region may serve as a key determinant in PopZ to regulate its association with (known and unknown) client proteins and its bipolar localization and/or dynamics.
source: Thus, the DUF2497 region may serve as a key determinant in PopZ to regulate its association with (known and unknown) client proteins and its bipolar localization and/or dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: The bipolar localization of DivIVA of the Gram-positive Firmicutes is governed by the biophysical properties of DivIVA that attract it to concavely curved membranes.
source: The bipolar localization of DivIVA of the Gram-positive Firmicutes has been intensively studied and is governed by the biophysical properties of DivIVA that attract it to concavely curved membranes and thus both cell poles when expressed in E. coli (Lenarcic et al., 2009; Ramamurthi and Losick, 2009; Strahl and Hamoen, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The α-proteobacterial PopZ system is of distinct ancestry and structural features compared to DivIVA.
source: The α-proteobacterial PopZ system is of distinct ancestry and structural features compared to DivIVA, and it aggregates into (sporadic) monopolar and non-polar (cytoplasmic) clusters in (filamentous) E. coli in the absence of ZitP.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between PopZ and DivIVA.

claim: PopZ aggregates into (sporadic) monopolar and non-polar (cytoplasmic) clusters in (filamentous) E. coli in the absence of ZitP.
source: The α-proteobacterial PopZ system is of distinct ancestry and structural features compared to DivIVA, and it aggregates into (sporadic) monopolar and non-polar (cytoplasmic) clusters in (filamentous) E. coli in the absence of ZitP.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments.

claim: The robust assembly of (near native) bipolar PopZ•ZitP complexes at the polar membrane is observed by PALM.
source: A clearly different mechanism underlies the robust assembly of (near native) bipolar PopZ•ZitP complexes at the polar membrane as observed by PALM.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from PALM experiments.

claim: Bipolar PopZ•ZitP complexes in E. coli can be reconstituted with components from different α-proteobacteria.
source: As these bipolar PopZ•ZitP complexes in E. coli can also be reconstituted with components from different α-proteobacteria, it is unlikely that it is mediated by specialized phospholipids as the composition differs between E. coli, Caulobacterales (De Siervo, 1985; De Siervo and Homola, 1980) and other α-proteobacteria, for example the Rickettsiales.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from heterologous localization experiments.

claim: Rickettsial ZitP retains PopZ control activities, suggesting that obligate intracellular pathogens also feature a polarized PopZ•ZitP complex.
source: There are intriguing evolutionary implications based on the finding that rickettsial ZitP retains the aforementioned PopZ control activities. It suggests that these obligate intracellular pathogens also feature a polarized PopZ•ZitP complex.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the findings.

claim: The rickettsial actin filament organizer Sca2 is polarized and promotes actin-mediated motility of some Rickettsiae inside the host cell cytoplasm.
source: The rickettsial actin filament organizer Sca2 is polarized and promotes actin-mediated motility of some Rickettsiae inside the host cell cytoplasm (Haglund et al., 2010; Madasu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The PopZ•ZitP bipolarity system may have served as a primordial platform for the acquisition of specialized polarity based functions conferred via PopZ-interacting proteins.
source: It is therefore conceivable that the PopZ•ZitP bipolarity system served as a primordial platform (Figure 6H) for the acquisition of specialized polarity based functions conferred via PopZ-interacting proteins that reinforce bipolarity and/or confer other polarized traits.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: PopZ is required for stalk biogenesis in C. crescentus.
source: For example, PopZ is also required for stalk biogenesis in C. crescentus (Bowman et al., 2010), a structure that requires specialized peptidoglycan (PG) biosynthesis enzymes (Kühn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several Rhizobiales members sequester PopZ to the site of PG synthesis to promote unipolar growth.
source: As several Rhizobiales members also sequester PopZ to the site of PG synthesis to promote unipolar growth (Anderson-Furgeson et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2012; Curtis and Brun, 2014; Grangeon et al., 2015), the current challenge is to determine which proteins interact with PopZ in the different α-proteobacterial branches, particularly in the Rhizobiales.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PopZ is unipolar in the Rhizobiales and no ZitP orthologs are encoded, suggesting that unknown PopZ-control mechanisms exist.
source: PopZ is unipolar in this branch (Deghelt et al., 2014; Grangeon et al., 2015) and no ZitP orthologs are encoded, suggesting that unknown PopZ-control mechanisms exist (Figure 6H,Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from genomic and localization observations.

claim: Many members of the Rhodobacterales do not encode a conspicuous PopZ ortholog in their genome.
source: By contrast, many members of the Rhodobacterales, do not encode a conspicuous PopZ ortholog in their genome.
evidence: This is stated as a genomic observation.

claim: The structural divergence of the ZitPZnR in the Rhodobacterales suggests that ZitP has been appropriated for other functions or interactions with partners differing in primary structure.
source: This, along with the structural divergence of the ZitPZnR in this lineage (Figure 3C), suggests that ZitP has been appropriated for other functions or interactions with partners differing in primary structure.

claim: Proper control of polarization is critical for efficient cellular proliferation and fitness in many cell types.
